angle: An AI cleanup of 3 years of renewal data showed the renewal rate was worse than the board was told
linkedin_post:
3 years of renewals went untracked.

Then an AI cleanup showed the real renewal rate.

Jeff Ignacio cleaned up a company's renewal database after the renewal process had been neglected for 3 years. Renewals from 2023 to 2024 were missing entirely.

The fix started with reconciling against Stripe data. Customers were still paying, so payments became the source of truth.

From there, Jeff rebuilt the 2025 renewal base from those payments. Then built closed-lost opportunities so win rate analysis on renewals was possible.

The result: the renewal rate was much worse than the company had been telling its board.

Not a happy outcome. But that's the ROI of clean data. The reaction goes from "we think we're fine" to "we're churning customers, hands on deck, plug this gap."

You can't fix a leak you aren't measuring.

When did you last audit your renewal data?
carousel: Slide 1: A company neglected its renewal process for 3 years.
Slide 2: Renewals from 2023 to 2024 were missing entirely.
Slide 3: Jeff Ignacio reconciled the gaps against Stripe payment data.
Slide 4: Customers were still paying, so payments became the truth.
Slide 5: The 2025 renewal base was rebuilt from those payments.
Slide 6: Closed-lost opps were built to run renewal win rates.
Slide 7: The renewal rate was far worse than the board was told.
Slide 8: Bad news, but it put hands on deck to plug the gap.

lesson.title: Clean renewal data shows the real churn story
takeaways: When CRM data is neglected, billing data like Stripe can serve as the source of truth for who is actually paying.
Rebuilding renewal records and closed-lost opportunities makes renewal win rate analysis possible.
Uncomfortable numbers are the ROI: they trigger action before more customers churn.
lesson.exercise: Pick your last 12 months of renewals and match each one against billing data. Count how many are missing or wrong in your CRM, then recalculate your renewal rate from payments.

angle: The deals that 'close this month' and never do: how I stopped doing slipped-deal postmortems by hand
post_first_line: Every week, the same deal slips.
linkedin_post:
Every week, the same deal slips.

I used to walk into forecast calls with the postmortem done by hand, and it never told me enough.

Anyone who's worked in RevOps knows the pattern. A rep says it will close this month. It's sitting in commit. It never closes.

My old process was asking the rep why it slipped, then bringing that answer to the leadership call. That gives you one person's version of the story.

So I built something different. I point an agent at the Attention calls and tell it to run a postmortem on every call tied to the deal. It reads the SPICE notes and tells me what was missing. It also tells me what risk the rep actually flagged.

Then it checks my calendar for the next forecast leadership meeting. Before that meeting, it drops the analysis into Slack.

The write-up covers the original close date, the root cause, and where the rep missed something.

I no longer walk in saying "this deal slipped." I walk in with the reason it slipped, backed by the calls.

The rep's explanation is only one input. The calls tell you the rest.

How do you review slipped deals today?
carousel: Slide 1: Deals that 'close this month' and never do.
Slide 2: Asking the rep why it slipped gives you one version.
Slide 3: I pointed an agent at every call on the deal.
Slide 4: It reads the SPICE notes and finds what was missing.
Slide 5: It surfaces the risk the rep actually flagged.
Slide 6: It checks my calendar for the next forecast meeting.
Slide 7: The postmortem lands in Slack before that meeting starts.
Slide 8: Original close date, root cause, and where the rep missed.

lesson.title: Automate the slipped-deal postmortem
takeaways: Rep explanations are one input. Call recordings and notes give the fuller picture.
Timing matters: deliver the analysis before the forecast meeting, in the place people already read.
A consistent format (original close date, root cause, rep miss) makes slippage patterns easy to compare.
lesson.exercise: Pick the last three deals that slipped out of commit. Go through the calls and notes on each, and write down the original close date, the root cause, and the risk the rep flagged or missed. Then see which steps you could hand to an agent.

caption: Stop hand-writing slipped deal postmortems

angle: I vibe coded my own Salesforce MCP connector so you don't have to. Here's the workaround
post_first_line: I vibe coded a Salesforce MCP connector.
linkedin_post:
I vibe coded a Salesforce MCP connector.

I would not recommend it to anyone.

I went deep down this rabbit hole because I needed an MCP that could read Salesforce data and give me real analysis. Not a demo. The real thing.

The first thing you need is a connector with an MCP that can read a database, so you get the schema. CData is one of those connectors.

I skipped that path and built my own instead. That meant writing Apex code and deploying it. A lot of grinding for something that already had an easier route.

There are better ways. You can put a middleware layer in between that feeds the data in, and you still get the analysis in the meantime.

This was a real pain I went through, so you don't have to repeat it.

Where have you over-built something that already existed?
carousel: Slide 1: I vibe coded my own Salesforce MCP connector. Don't.
Slide 2: The goal: an MCP that reads Salesforce and gives real analysis.
Slide 3: Step one is a connector with an MCP that reads a database.
Slide 4: That gives you the schema. CData is one option.
Slide 5: I went deeper and built my own, writing Apex code.
Slide 6: Then I had to deploy it. Far more work than expected.
Slide 7: The workaround: middleware that feeds the data in for analysis.
Slide 8: Buy the plumbing. Spend your time on the analysis.

lesson.title: Don't build the Salesforce MCP connector yourself
takeaways: You need a connector with an MCP that can read a database so you get the schema. CData is one example.
Building your own means writing and deploying Apex code, which is a rabbit hole.
Middleware that feeds data in lets you get analysis in the meantime.
lesson.exercise: List the data connections your AI workflow needs. For each one, check for an existing connector or middleware option before you write any code.

angle: Stop writing your own prompts: have Claude rewrite them using your CRM schema
linkedin_post:
Stop writing your own prompts.
I let Claude rewrite mine, and the result was better than anything I'd have typed.

I have a skill I call with a prompt enhancer command. I give it my rough prompt, and I'd say there's a fair amount of context in it already.

Claude went into my metadata and the Salesforce schema. It figured out that when I say "new business," I'm referring to opportunity type: new business.

That one translation matters. It excludes expansions, renewals, and all of that. It also pulled in the forecast category names.

Then it broke the prompt apart into the original ask, the intent, and the action that needs to happen.

We use SPICE internally, and there are notes for it in the setup. Claude went in and found the fields that apply to it. That part was mind-blowing.

I used to think good prompting meant getting better at wording. Now I think it means giving the model your schema and letting it do the translating.

What's one prompt you'd hand off to Claude first?
carousel: Slide 1: Stop writing your own prompts. Delegate it to Claude.
Slide 2: I built a skill that acts as a prompt enhancer.
Slide 3: Claude reads your metadata and the Salesforce schema first.
Slide 4: "New business" becomes opportunity type: new business.
Slide 5: Expansions and renewals get excluded automatically.
Slide 6: It splits your prompt into original ask, intent, and action.
Slide 7: It even finds the fields that apply to SPICE.
Slide 8: Give the model your schema. Let it translate.

lesson.title: Let Claude rewrite your prompts using your CRM schema
takeaways: Claude can read your metadata and Salesforce schema to turn vague wording into precise CRM terms, like mapping "new business" to opportunity type new business.
A good enhanced prompt separates the original ask, the intent, and the action needed.
If you have an internal methodology like SPICE, Claude can find the relevant fields on its own.
lesson.exercise: Create a prompt enhancer skill in Claude. Run one rough CRM prompt through it and compare the rewrite with your original. Note which fields and filters it added.

caption: Let Claude write your prompts

angle: Don't use your smartest model for every step. Scoring 15,000 accounts of sales calls cost about $30
post_first_line: $30 to score 15,000 accounts of sales calls.
linkedin_post:
$30 to score 15,000 accounts of sales calls.

The trick is knowing which step does not need your smartest model.

Jeff Ignacio shared how to run this kind of analysis without burning budget. For the classification step, skip Claude Sonnet. Use a lower-level model like Claude Haiku. If you're bold, something like DeepSeek on a Fireworks API works too.

That swap dramatically brings down costs. Jeff's estimate was about $30 to analyze the entire history of one sales team's calls.

Then the interesting part starts. You can see what the MEDDIC score averaged across the team, then run a time series. Did this rep improve over time?

You can compare regrettable attrition against non-regrettable attrition. Was there a difference between the two? Did improvement in MEDDIC correlate with improvement in performance?

Those are second, third, and fourth order questions. Most teams never get to them because they are still busy building surface level reporting.

Cheap models for the repetitive steps. Save the expensive thinking for the questions that matter.

Which step in your workflow is overpaying for intelligence?
carousel: Slide 1: Scoring 15,000 accounts of sales calls cost about $30.
Slide 2: Don't use your smartest model for every step.
Slide 3: Classification is a job for Claude Haiku, not Sonnet.
Slide 4: Feeling bold? Try DeepSeek on a Fireworks API.
Slide 5: Cheaper models dramatically bring down your costs.
Slide 6: Then run a time series: did each rep improve?
Slide 7: Compare regrettable and non-regrettable attrition. Spot any difference?
Slide 8: Stop stopping at surface level reporting. Ask deeper questions.

lesson.title: Match the model to the step
takeaways: Classification steps don't need your most powerful model. A lower-level model like Claude Haiku can do the job.
Lower model costs make large-scale analysis practical: about $30 for 15,000 accounts in Jeff's estimate.
Cheap analysis frees you to ask second, third, and fourth order questions beyond surface level reporting.
lesson.exercise: List the steps in one AI workflow you run today. Mark which are simple classification and test a cheaper model on those, then compare cost and output quality.

caption: $30 for 15,000 accounts

angle: Leadership analyses that took a week now take a couple of hours, and that's how RevOps proves AI ROI
post_first_line: One week down to a couple of hours.
linkedin_post:
One week down to a couple of hours.

That's the shift I'm seeing in how RevOps proves AI ROI.

The analyses I put together for leadership used to take me about a week. Now they take a couple of hours.

The result is that leadership makes decisions much faster than they used to. That speed is the ROI, and leadership can see it.

Then I take it one step further. I put a dollar amount on it, and I have Claude help me do that.

When you show the ROI in dollars, you're speaking the language leadership already uses. That's when the ROI starts to get proven.
